strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: cooperative multi-agent control with irregular decision intervals, using an HJB critic and gradient consistency regularization.
Reports experiments across eight MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo settings with multiple random seeds, showing promising returns on several tasks.
Includes useful ablations of gradient regularization, critic loss components, and activation functions, plus network architecture and hyperparameter tables.
weaknesses: The central convergence theorem is false under its stated assumptions. Bounded dynamics Jacobians do not imply contraction. Appendix A.5 claims that sufficiently small Δt makes exp(-ρΔt)(1+LfΔt)<1, but this expression equals 1+(Lf-ρ)Δt+O(Δt²). For scalar dynamics f(x)=2x and ρ=0.95, the proposed map is expansive for sufficiently small positive steps. Moreover, contraction of a fixed affine map would not establish convergence of the jointly trained neural critic, dynamics model, and changing policies.

The defining VGI equation uses the wrong Jacobian for continuous dynamics. Given x_next=x+f(x,u)Δt+O(Δt²), gradient propagation requires [I+Δt ∂f/∂x]ᵀ, whereas Eq. (11) and Appendix A.4 use (∂f/∂x)ᵀ. Appendix A.5 silently switches to the former expression. The learned next-state predictor in Section 3.4 could support a valid discrete-transition target, but that does not validate the stated continuous-time derivation or theorem.

Lemma 3.3 asserts pointwise policy improvement after one sufficiently small actor-gradient step, but Appendix A.3 instead assumes exact statewise greedy maximization of Q. A sampled gradient step with shared neural parameters and an approximate critic does not satisfy that assumption. Thus the proof does not establish the claimed guarantee for the proposed algorithm.

The analytical ground truth used to validate value and gradient accuracy is inconsistent with the objective. Appendix B.1 defines negative quadratic rewards but uses the positive LQR cost xᵀPx as the optimal reward value; the corresponding reward value and gradient should have opposite signs. Its Riccati equation also omits the stated discount rate, and unconstrained LQR is not generally exact under the specified action bounds. These issues undermine the central accuracy comparisons in Figures 1, 3, and 9.

The control objective is inconsistent across sections. Eq. (2) defines an infinite-horizon stationary discounted value, while Lemma 3.1 imposes a finite-horizon terminal condition. Appendix A.1 introduces an undiscounted terminal payoff, although the displayed discounted HJB corresponds to discounting that payoff relative to the current time. The resulting value target is not specified coherently.

The empirical comparisons do not establish competitiveness against strong modern MARL methods. Main benchmarks compare primarily with adapted continuous-time methods; MADDPG appears only in the oscillator experiment. Comparisons with MAPPO and appropriately time-aware discrete-time baselines, together with baseline adaptation and tuning details, are needed to substantiate the broader claims.

Evidence for accurate gradients and robust temporal generalization is limited. Figure 3 uses separate color scales, and VIP's value range is substantially narrower than the ground-truth range; visual resemblance does not demonstrate accurate recovery. Aggregate value/gradient errors are missing, and the time-interval robustness experiment is confined to the oscillator rather than the main benchmarks.

Important reproducibility details remain unspecified or inconsistent: numerical critic-loss weights, MPE time-interval bounds, terminal targets, baseline architectures and tuning, and reward/time normalization. Actor equations and pseudocode condition on global state, whereas Table 2 specifies local observations and the time interval, leaving the claimed decentralized execution protocol unclear.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: cooperative multi-agent control with irregular decision intervals, where accurate value gradients may improve learning.
Combining an HJB-based critic with gradient-consistency supervision is a plausible practical approach. The reported experiments span eight MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo tasks and generally favor VIP.
Includes useful ablations of VGI, critic loss components, and activation functions, alongside an analytical oscillator example and architectural details.
weaknesses: The central convergence guarantee is false under the stated assumptions. Theorem 3.4 assumes only a bounded dynamics Jacobian, which does not imply contraction. Appendix A.5 claims that sufficiently small Δt makes exp(-ρΔt)(1 + LfΔt) < 1, but this expression is 1 + (Lf - ρ)Δt + O(Δt²), and exceeds one for sufficiently small positive Δt when Lf > ρ. Additional stability or discount-dominance assumptions are essential; the claimed guarantee is therefore unsupported.

The core VGI derivation conflates continuous dynamics with a discrete transition map. For x_next = x + f(x,u)Δt, differentiating the Bellman target requires the Jacobian I + Δt∂f/∂x, whereas Equation (11) and Appendix A.4 use ∂f/∂x alone. Appendix A.5 switches to the correct Euler Jacobian without reconciling the difference. The learned next-state model in Section 3.4.1 could support a valid discrete gradient target, but that does not establish the equations or theorem presented.

Lemma 3.3 claims pointwise policy improvement after one sufficiently small actor-gradient step, but Appendix A.3 instead assumes exact greedy maximization of the old Q-function. These are different updates. Improvement of an aggregate policy objective does not generally guarantee improvement at every state-action pair, particularly with shared function approximation and an approximate critic.

The analytical validation does not consistently match the stated objective. Equation (2) defines an infinite-horizon discounted reward, while Lemma 3.1 introduces a finite-horizon terminal condition. Appendix B.1 then uses an undiscounted Riccati equation and positive V = xᵀPx despite defining rewards as negative quadratic costs. Action bounds introduce another qualification to exact LQR optimality. These discrepancies undermine the claimed ground-truth value and gradient comparisons unless the transformations and assumptions are explicitly reconciled.

The main comparisons omit strong contemporary MARL baselines such as MAPPO and FACMAC, as well as direct comparisons with the cited PINN-based continuous-time methods. MADDPG appears only in the oscillator study. There is no convincing comparison against interval-conditioned discrete-time methods using time-consistent rewards and discounts, and adaptation and tuning details for the continuous-time baselines are insufficient.

The evaluation does not establish the broad claims about time-resolution robustness or scalability. Irregular intervals are evaluated, but controlled training-to-test interval shifts are limited to the toy example. Physical-time horizons and reward integration are insufficiently specified: episodes use 50 steps despite variable durations, while benchmark reward structures are reportedly unchanged. No systematic agent-count, state-dimension, runtime, or memory scaling study supports the claim of mitigating the curse of dimensionality.

Reproducibility and empirical interpretation remain incomplete. Numerical loss weights, MPE interval bounds, terminal targets, baseline tuning, and the meaning of shaded uncertainty bands are not adequately specified. The text reports five seeds while Table 1 lists seeds 111–120. Figure 3 uses substantially different color scales, and VIP's displayed gradient range remains shifted from the reference, so qualitative similarity does not establish the claimed accurate recovery. Aggregate value/gradient errors with uncertainty are needed.

The VGI equations are inconsistent. Equation (11) propagates gradients through the Jacobian of the continuous-time vector field, whereas Euler integration requires I+Δt∇f, as Appendix A.5 itself uses. strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: cooperative multi-agent control with irregular decision intervals, where accurate value gradients can improve policy learning.
Reports promising learning curves across eight MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo settings, with comparisons against continuous-time and discrete-time baselines.
Includes useful ablations of gradient supervision, critic losses, and activation functions, alongside an analytical control example.
weaknesses: The central convergence guarantee is false under the stated assumptions. Theorem 3.4 assumes only a bounded dynamics Jacobian, which does not establish contraction. Appendix A.5 claims that sufficiently small Δt ensures exp(-ρΔt)(1 + LfΔt) < 1, but this expression exceeds one for sufficiently small positive Δt when Lf > ρ. Moreover, autonomous dynamics do not imply a constant Jacobian along a trajectory. These errors invalidate the claimed VGI convergence proof.

The core VGI estimator is inconsistent with its derivation. With f defined as the continuous-time vector field, differentiating the Euler transition requires I + Δt∇xf, whereas Equations 10–11 use ∇xf directly. Appendix A.5 switches to the former expression without reconciling the difference. The learned next-state model in Section 3.4 could explain an implementation using a transition Jacobian, but it does not repair the stated definition or theorem.

Lemma 3.3 claims pointwise policy improvement after a sufficiently small gradient step, but Appendix A.3 instead assumes exact greedy maximization of the old Q-function. An expected policy-gradient update with shared parameters and an approximate critic does not imply improvement at every state-action pair. The proof therefore establishes a different result from the claimed guarantee.

The analytical ground truth is inconsistent with the objective. Appendix B.1 specifies negative quadratic rewards but reports the positive cost-to-go xᵀPx as the optimal value. Its Riccati equation also omits the discount term required by the paper's discounted objective, and unconstrained LQR is not generally exact under bounded actions. Consequently, the central value and gradient accuracy comparisons cannot be accepted as validated ground-truth tests.

The variable-interval dynamics model omits the interval from its inputs: Equation 13 predicts x(t+Δt) from only (x,u), and Table 2 confirms this architecture. Different sampled intervals generally yield different next states for identical inputs. Dividing this prediction's displacement by the observed Δt does not resolve that ambiguity, undermining the claimed treatment of irregular timing.

The baseline evaluation does not establish whether gains persist against time-aware discrete-time methods using interval-dependent discounts, integrated rewards, and matched interval information. Such Bellman formulations can handle irregular decision times. Baseline adaptation and tuning are insufficiently documented, while episode-based comparisons lack corresponding physical-time and computational-cost measurements.

Reproducibility and the multi-agent interpretation remain unclear. The formulation and algorithm condition actors on the global state despite claiming decentralized execution, whereas Table 2 specifies local observations. Numerical loss weights, MPE interval bounds, and uncertainty-band definitions are missing; the text reports five seeds while the hyperparameter table lists ten. The promised code link has no usable destination in the supplied PDF. Together with the mathematical errors, these gaps prevent verification of the reported results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: cooperative multi-agent control under irregular decision intervals, where accurate value gradients can matter substantially.

Combining an HJB residual, a value-bootstrap anchor, and gradient-consistency supervision is a plausible practical approach. The reported experiments cover eight MPE and MuJoCo settings and show benefits from VGI.
The evaluation includes several continuous-time and discrete-time baselines, component ablations, activation comparisons, and timestep sensitivity experiments.
weaknesses: The central convergence guarantee is false under the stated assumptions. Theorem 3.4 assumes only a bounded dynamics Jacobian, which does not imply contraction. Appendix A.5 claims that sufficiently small Δt makes β = exp(-ρΔt)(1 + LfΔt) < 1, but β = 1 + (Lf - ρ)Δt + O(Δt²), so this fails for small positive steps when Lf > ρ. Moreover, autonomous dynamics do not imply that their Jacobian is constant along a trajectory. The proof therefore establishes neither the stated contraction nor convergence of the trained neural critic.

The defining VGI equations confuse the vector field with the state-transition map. For dynamics ẋ = f(x,u), differentiating an Euler transition requires the Jacobian I + Δt∂f/∂x. Equations 10–11 and Appendix A.4 instead use ∂f/∂x directly, whereas Appendix A.5 silently introduces the missing identity and timestep. Section 3.4's learned next-state model could make the implementation's gradient target sensible, but that interpretation does not repair the stated definition and theorem. This inconsistency affects the main proposed contribution.

Lemma 3.3 does not justify the actual actor update. It asserts pointwise Q-function improvement after a sufficiently small policy-gradient step, while Appendix A.3 assumes an exact greedy maximization of Q. Those are different operations; improving an expected surrogate with shared policy parameters and an approximate critic does not generally improve Q at every state-action pair.

The analytical ground truth used to validate value and gradient accuracy is inconsistent with the formulated objective. Appendix B.1 specifies negative quadratic rewards but reports the positive cost value V*(x) = xᵀPx and gradient 2Px. Its Riccati equation also omits the discount term -ρP required by the discounted objective, and unconstrained LQR is not globally exact under the stated action bounds. These issues undermine the central value-accuracy demonstrations in Figures 1 and 3.

The learned dynamics model is not adequately specified for irregular intervals. Equation 13 predicts the next state from only state and action, although that target also depends on the randomly sampled Δt; Table 2 likewise omits Δt from the dynamics input. Dividing this prediction's displacement by the realized Δt does not generally recover the vector field. This creates a substantive mismatch between the motivating setting and the model used by both HJB and VGI losses.

The experiments do not isolate an advantage over appropriately time-aware discrete-time methods. The paper does not establish that the baselines use interval-dependent discounts exp(-ρΔt), consistent reward integration, or equivalent interval information. Bellman backups can accommodate variable durations. Figure 8 additionally compares against MADDPG trained under a discrete-time setting, making transfer mismatch a competing explanation. The strong claims about inherent discrete-time failure are consequently unsupported.

Reproducibility and the multi-agent interpretation remain incomplete. The derivations and algorithm condition every actor on global state, while Table 2 specifies local observations plus the interval, leaving decentralized execution unclear. Numerical loss-weight settings, the MPE interval range, and sufficient details of baseline adaptations are missing; the main text reports five seeds while the appendix lists ten. Reported learning curves cannot resolve the mathematical and reference-solution problems above.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: cooperative control with high-frequency or irregular decision intervals. Explicitly improving critic gradients is a plausible and useful research direction.
Reports promising results across eight MPE and multi-agent MuJoCo settings, with continuous-time and discrete-time baselines and five-seed experiments.
Includes useful ablations of gradient consistency, critic losses, and activation functions, plus an analytical control example intended to assess value-gradient accuracy.
weaknesses: The central convergence guarantee is false under the stated assumptions. In Appendix A.5, bounded dynamics Jacobians and small Δt do not imply β = exp(-ρΔt)(1 + LfΔt) < 1: β = 1 + (Lf - ρ)Δt + O(Δt²), which exceeds one for sufficiently small positive Δt when Lf > ρ. Moreover, autonomous dynamics do not imply a constant Jacobian along changing states and actions. Thus Theorem 3.4 does not establish the claimed convergence.

The core VGI definition is inconsistent with its derivation. For the continuous-time vector field f, differentiating an Euler transition requires the Jacobian I + Δt∇xf, whereas Eqs. 10–12 use ∇xf alone. Appendix A.5 inserts the missing terms and therefore analyzes a different update. Section 3.4 instead learns a next-state map, whose Jacobian could justify the implemented target, but the manuscript must distinguish these objects and provide a consistent algorithm and theorem.

Lemma 3.3 claims pointwise policy improvement after a small gradient step with an approximate critic. Appendix A.3 instead assumes exact greedy maximization of the old policy's Q-function. That assumption does not describe the proposed actor update, and improvement of an expected surrogate does not guarantee improvement at every state-action pair.

The analytical ground truth is inconsistent with the stated objective. Appendix B.1 uses a negative quadratic reward but gives the positive cost value xᵀPx and gradient 2Px as reward-value targets. Its Riccati equation also omits the discount term required by the discounted objective. Consequently, the value and gradient comparisons do not establish accuracy against the claimed optimal value function.

The learned transition model omits the variable time interval from its inputs: Eq. 13 and Table 2 predict the next state from only state and action, although the next state depends on the randomly sampled interval. Dividing this prediction's displacement by the realized interval does not generally recover the correct vector field. This directly affects the proposed irregular-time setting and requires clarification or correction.

The baseline comparisons do not establish whether gains come from VGI or unequal treatment of elapsed time. The paper does not adequately document interval-dependent discounting, reward integration, time inputs, or tuning for the discrete-time baselines, nor the multi-agent adaptations of the continuous-time methods. Time-aware Bellman backups are possible, so the claim that discrete-time backups inherently require fixed intervals is too strong.

The decentralized-execution claim is insufficiently specified: the formulation, actor equations, and pseudocode condition each actor on the global state, while Table 2 specifies local observations. Reproducibility is also limited by missing numerical loss-weight settings and MPE interval bounds, inconsistent seed reporting, and no clear definition of plotted uncertainty. These gaps compound the fundamental mathematical problems and prevent the reported empirical gains from supporting acceptance.
